strengths: Extensive empirical evaluation: eight diverse benchmarks, 15 open-source LLMs, and comparisons against five closed-source models and six collaboration baselines (Table 1), with an additional experiment at 32K output tokens (Table 5) that strengthens the robustness of the claims.

The framework is well-motivated and reasonably complete: retrieval-based prior selection (RPS) over an instance-level capability matrix, plus an exploration–exploitation posterior stage with multiple aggregations and a hybrid similarity/perplexity score, directly addresses the scalability and exploration limitations identified in prior MACS work.

Good supporting analyses: component ablations (Table 2), scaling curves with increasing LLM count (Fig. 3), cross-dataset retrieval analysis (Fig. 4), a pairwise ranking score comparing prior estimates against Symbolic-MoE (Table 3), posterior drop analysis (Fig. 5), and aggregator-selection analysis (Fig. 6).

Implementation details are documented at an above-average level of specificity: model bank, sampling configs, embedding model, and all key hyperparameters (K, Nsup_base, gamma, Kdrop, n, lambda) are reported in Appendix A.3, and prompts are given in the appendix, aiding reproducibility.
The limitations section is candid about computational cost and uniform inference configuration.
weaknesses: Compute-unfair headline comparison. The central claim 'open-source collaboration beats closed-source LLMs' compares a system that invokes ~7 referencers plus n=8 aggregator calls (roughly 15+ LLM inferences per question, plus question-bank evaluation of all 15 LLMs) against single-call closed-source models. Self-Consistency and Self-MoA baselines use only 8 samples of one model. Without matched-compute or cost-matched baselines, the 'pushing the upper bound of intelligence' framing is overclaimed; a simple best-of-15 repeated sampling baseline is missing.

Potential validation–test proximity inflates gains. The question bank is built from validation splits of the same benchmarks (e.g., AIME 1983–2023 problems for AIME2024; MBPP train+val), so retrieval for a test question surfaces very similar or near-duplicate items. The paper does not report performance under a distribution-shifted or cross-domain retrieval setting, so generalization claims are weakly supported.

No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals. Several benchmarks are tiny (AIME2024 has 30 items; differences of one question swing results by 3.3 points), and SMACS is below the open-source upper bound on GPQA, LiveCodeBench, and MedMCQA despite average-based claims of 'exceeding upper bounds'.

Signs of cherry-picking: the aggregator switches from Llama-3.3-70B to QwQ-32B specifically for coding tasks in the 32K-token experiment (A.5), and baselines like Simple Router are selected from question-bank performance. There are also internal inconsistencies (e.g., closed-source IFEval upper bound of 88.50 in Table 1 while the best listed closed-source score is 88.00).

Technical clarity issues: Eq. (3) is garbled (gamma * max_Nsup_base(S^in) mixes threshold and base count), Eq. (6) is hard to parse, S^PPL = 1 - PPL is ill-defined (perplexity is unbounded and it is unclear which model computes it), and the text contains numerous typos ('strengthes', 'a embed', 'It explore', 'vallina'), suggesting a lack of polishing.

Novelty is moderate: the work combines known ingredients (retrieval-based routing, MoA-style aggregation, similarity/perplexity-based selection) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; the interesting tension with Self-MoA's finding that single-model ensembles suffice is not deeply analyzed.

No code or question bank is released at submission time ('Code will be released'), limiting reproducibility of an experimentally heavy system; Figure 1 radar plots are unreadable at the rendered scale.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely question: whether ensembles of open-source LLMs, orchestrated at inference time, can match or exceed flagship closed-source models.

The proposed framework is clearly decomposed (retrieval-based prior selection; exploration via prior-based dropping of references; exploitation via a hybrid similarity/perplexity selection score), and the method section gives enough mathematical detail (Eqs. 1–7, hyperparameters in A.3) to follow the pipeline end-to-end.

The experimental scope is broad: eight benchmarks, fifteen open-source models, comparisons against five closed-source models and six collaboration baselines, plus a scaling study (Fig. 3), component ablations (Table 2), retrieval-provenance analysis (Fig. 4), a pairwise-ranking analysis of prior quality (Table 3), posterior-drop analysis (Fig. 5), and aggregator-selection analysis (Fig. 6).

The analysis of aggregator selection (Appendix A.4) — showing that aggregation ability is partially dissociated from single-model accuracy — is an interesting empirical observation beyond the main claim.
weaknesses: A central validity concern is potential distributional leakage between the question bank and the test sets. The question bank is built from the validation splits of the *same* benchmarks used for testing, and RPS retrieves the most similar bank questions per test query. Performance gains may therefore partly reflect access to near-distribution solved exemplars rather than generalizable 'intelligence upper bound' gains, yet there is no experiment isolating SMACS on truly unseen/out-of-distribution questions, and no control (e.g., routing with generic question banks) to quantify this.

The headline claim ('beats closed-source LLMs', 'pushing the upper bound of intelligence') is not cost-fair: SMACS runs 7 referencers (20B–72B) plus 8 aggregations per question, orders of magnitude more inference compute than a single closed-source model. The paper acknowledges the efficiency limitation but the abstract and title do not convey that the comparison is compute-asymmetric, which is misleading.

Statistical rigor is weak. Several test sets are tiny (AIME 2024 has 30 items; GPQA-Diamond ~200), so differences of one question move AIME by 3.33 points, yet no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported anywhere, despite many claims of small margins (e.g., +2.04% over the closed-source upper bound).

Evaluation protocol for the closed-source baselines is under-specified: all models are sampled at temperature 0.7 with 8,192 max tokens, which is non-standard for benchmark reporting and may disadvantage baselines; several reported closed-source numbers (e.g., Claude-3.7-Sonnet at 26.70 on AIME) look implausibly low relative to commonly reported results, raising questions about prompting/answer-extraction fairness. It is unclear whether closed-source models were evaluated by the authors or numbers were taken from elsewhere.

Internal inconsistencies undermine confidence in the results: Table 1 lists the closed-source IFEval upper bound as 88.50 while Claude-3.5-Sonnet and the open-source upper bound rows show 88.00/90.00; SMACS ties the IFEval score of its own aggregator (90.00), suggesting the system adds nothing on that benchmark; the ablation 'baseline' configuration (79.60% MMLU-PRO) is never defined; and Eq. 7's perplexity score '1 − PPL' is unbounded and it is never stated which model computes PPL for aggregated responses — a cross-model PPL comparison would be ill-founded.

Novelty is limited: the components are largely recombinations of existing techniques — retrieval over recorded per-question accuracy (routing à la Shnitzer et al. 2023 / RouterDC), MoA-style aggregation, and best-of-n selection with embedding-similarity and perplexity scores. The 'exploration–exploitation' framing restyles simple subset sampling; no new algorithmic machinery is introduced.

Reproducibility is not established: the code-release URL is missing/empty in the manuscript, the closed-source evaluation scripts and retrieval index construction are not described in enough detail to replicate, and there are numerous typos and notational glitches (Eq. 3 is garbled as written; 'strengthes', 'vallina', inconsistent 'SMAS' vs 'SMACS'), indicating the paper was not carefully polished.

The scaling experiment (Fig. 3) conflates two effects: adding LLMs increases both the pool size and the fixed number of referencers/aggregations, so it does not cleanly support the claim of sustainable gains from model diversity.

strengths: The paper is well-organized around a clear prior/posterior decomposition of multi-agent collaboration, and the proposed SMACS framework (retrieval-based prior selection + exploration–exploitation posterior enhancement) is a reasonable and coherent combination of these two paradigms.

Experimental coverage is broad: eight mainstream benchmarks, fifteen heterogeneous open-source LLMs (20B–72B), and comparison against recent collaboration methods (Symbolic-MoE, MoA, Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting) under matched aggregator setups (Appendix A.3).

Reproducibility is comparatively strong for this line of work: dataset splits, the full LLM bank, inference configurations (vLLM, temperature, max tokens, embedding model), all key hyperparameters (K, N_sup_base, gamma, K_drop, n, lambda), and complete prompt templates are provided, with code promised.

Beyond headline results, the paper includes useful analyses: component ablations (Table 2), scalability curves as LLMs are added (Fig. 3), cross-dataset retrieval analysis (Fig. 4), a pairwise-ranking validation of the prior signal (Table 3), OCA/MCA analysis of the dropping strategies (Fig. 5), and aggregator-selection experiments (Fig. 6), plus an extended-token experiment (Table 5).
The limitations section is candid about the lack of efficiency optimization and uniform inference configurations.
weaknesses: The headline claim that SMACS 'beats closed-source LLMs' ignores the massive compute disparity: each query invokes ~7 referencer LLMs (20B–72B) plus ~8 aggregator calls, versus a single API call for GPT-4.1/o3-mini/Claude. No cost, latency, or tokens-per-query accounting is given, so the comparison is not apples-to-apples on either compute or financial budget.

The question bank is built from validation sets of the very benchmarks being tested (e.g., MMLU-Pro validation, GPQA non-diamond, MATH validation, AIME historical problems, LiveCodeBench v6), and Fig. 4 shows that most retrieved support questions come from the same benchmark as the test question. The prior signal is therefore largely benchmark-specific, and possible near-duplicate leakage between validation and test sets is never discussed, while closed-source baselines receive no analogous per-benchmark adaptation.

Several closed-source baseline numbers look anomalously low and are not validated (e.g., Claude-3.7-Sonnet at 26.70 on AIME and GPT-4o at 10.00, far below commonly reported scores). Since headline deltas (+12.73% over Claude-3.7-Sonnet) partly rest on these numbers, baseline evaluation methodology (answer extraction, thinking mode, decoding settings) needs justification.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or repeated runs are reported, despite small test sets (e.g., AIME with 30 questions, where a 6.67-point difference is one or two problems) and temperature-0.7 sampling.

Some experimental details are under-specified or ambiguous: which model computes the perplexity score in Eq. (7) is unclear (reference LLMs have different tokenizers), the 'baseline' configuration in Table 2 is not defined, and notation in Eqs. (3) and (6) is sloppy (e.g., gamma*max_{N_sup_base}(S_in)).

Novelty is modest: retrieval-based model selection closely resembles prior routing work (e.g., Shnitzer et al. 2023), and aggregation-by-an-LLM plus posterior scoring builds directly on MoA/Self-MoA; the contribution is a sensible integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
Writing quality needs work: typos ('strengthes', 'SMAS', 'vallina', 'It explore', 'a embed'), inconsistent terminology, and a cluttered Figure 2 impede readability.

The method is tuned per benchmark in places (custom prompts per benchmark in Fig. 7; a different aggregator for coding tasks in Appendix A.5), which further weakens the 'general system beats closed-source' framing.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: eight benchmarks spanning math, reasoning, instruction following, and code generation; fifteen open-source LLMs; comparisons against closed-source models and six multi-LLM collaboration methods.

Strong supporting analyses: component ablations (Table 10), cost-vs-accuracy trade-off curves over K, n, and Nsup_base (Tables 11-13), aggregator selection study (Fig. 7), OOD generalization experiments with stricter settings (Tables 3 and 7), perplexity scale analysis (Table 8), and repeated runs with standard deviations (Table 9).

The scalability claim is directly supported: Fig. 4 shows consistent gains as the LLM pool grows from 5 to 15 models, which is the paper's central selling point over prior routing/aggregation methods.

Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: full hyperparameters (K, Nsup_base, gamma, Kdrop, n, lambda), inference configurations, embedding model, dataset splits, complete LLM bank listing, and all prompts are provided in the appendix, and code release is claimed.

The proposed prior score is validated against actual test performance via a pairwise ranking metric (Table 4), going beyond end-task accuracy alone, and the retrieval composition analysis (Fig. 5) offers insight into cross-dataset capability transfer.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. RPS is essentially instance-level kNN routing over a question bank (close to Shnitzer et al. 2023-style benchmark-based routing), and EPE is MoA-style aggregation augmented with stochastic subset sampling and a heuristic similarity+PPL selection score. The contribution is a sensible combination of known ideas rather than a new method with strong conceptual grounding; the 'exploration-exploitation' framing is largely decorative.

Headline comparisons are somewhat misleading. The +5.36% over GPT-4.1 compares an ensemble of fifteen LLMs against a single model; the more meaningful margins over comparable ensemble baselines (Self-MoA +4.6%, Symbolic-MoE +5.14%, Self-Consistency +4.31%) are considerably smaller, and the 'exceeds the open-source upper bound' framing overclaims since an ensemble with an LLM aggregator naturally can surpass the best single model.

Potential information leakage: the unified question bank is built from validation sets of the very benchmarks used for testing, so retrieval may surface near-duplicate questions for test items. The OOD experiments (Tables 3, 7) partially mitigate this concern, but per-dataset performance in the main table may still be inflated relative to a genuinely unseen-task setting.

Baseline fairness is unclear: Symbolic-MoE is modified ('Symbolic-MoE*'), some baseline numbers (e.g., MoA at 70.51) appear below previously reported results, and the reported hyperparameter sensitivity results are internally inconsistent (peak performance at Nsup_base=200 in Table 13 while 400 is used as the default).

Presentation and rigor issues that undermine confidence: Eq. 3 is written incorrectly (the threshold expression 'gamma*max_{Nsup_base}(S^in)' does not parse as described in the text); the perplexity citation is a clearly erroneous placeholder ('Constituency Parsing. 2009. Speech and language processing. Power point slides'); the abstract's code URL is missing/truncated; there are numerous typos ('exploration', 'generate a aggregation', 'exploration-exploitation-driven' inconsistencies); notation is reused inconsistently (e.g., V^ref vs. V_hat^ref). The selection score is also evaluated on only two aggregators' PPL distributions (Table 8), so its general robustness is under-established.

Statistical significance is only reported for four of eight datasets with three seeds, and some test sets are small (AIME2024, n=30), where a single item moves accuracy by ~3.3 points; significance tests (e.g., paired bootstrap) are absent.

The hybrid posterior score (mean pairwise similarity + PPL) lacks theoretical or empirical motivation beyond ablation: high inter-aggregation similarity is assumed to correlate with quality, but no analysis of failure cases or of when similarity-based selection is misleading is provided.

strengths: Broad empirical coverage: eight mainstream benchmarks spanning math, reasoning, instruction following, and code generation, with a large pool of fifteen heterogeneous open-source LLMs (20B–72B).
Comparisons include multiple strong baselines (Symbolic-MoE, MoA, Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting, Simple Router) and leading closed-source models, plus cost/latency reporting.

Substantial auxiliary analyses in the appendix: component ablations (Table 10), accuracy-vs-cost curves for K, n, and Nsup_base, OOD question-bank experiments, aggregator-selection study, and repeated runs with standard deviations (Table 9).
Implementation details (hyperparameters, inference configs, prompts) are documented, and a code release is claimed.
The scaling analysis (Fig. 4) showing monotone gains as LLMs are added is a useful empirical observation.
weaknesses: Fairness/leakage concern that undermines the central claims: the unified question bank is constructed from the validation splits of the same eight benchmarks used for testing (Sec. 4.1), and RPS retrieves 'support questions' highly similar to each test question (Fig. 5 shows e.g. MBPP 97.4% retrieved from MBPP). The prior scores therefore nearly directly encode per-test-question model correctness, giving SMCS an information advantage unavailable to baselines. The OOD result (Table 3) that an MMLU-PRO-only bank nearly matches the full bank is presented as generalization but also suggests the mechanism is weakly discriminative.

Small test sets make headline claims statistically fragile: AIME has only 30 problems (73.33 = 22/30, so differences of ±3.33 are ±1 problem), GPQA-Diamond and IFEval subsets are similarly small; several claimed victories over GPT-o3-mini rest on one or two problems.

Compute asymmetry is downplayed: SMCS invokes 7 referencers plus 8 aggregation calls plus scoring per query, yet Table 2 reports SMCS at $8.11 vs Self-Consistency $8.39 — an accounting that seems inconsistent given the number of forward passes; the 'efficiency' story needs much more careful justification.

Comparisons against closed-source models conflate averages: the +5.36%/+5.28% claims are against averages including much weaker models (GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet), while SMCS actually loses to GPT-4.1 on MedMCQA and to GPT-o3-mini on LiveCodeBench in the main table.

Limited technical novelty: the system is essentially retrieval-based instance routing (closely related to prior routing work the authors themselves cite) combined with MoA-style multi-aggregation and best-of-n selection using perplexity + embedding-similarity scores. The 'exploration–exploitation' framing suggests a bandit/adaptive mechanism, but there is no learning or adaptive decision-making — it is fixed random subsetting plus scoring.

Notation and scholarship errors: Eq. (3) is garbled (the threshold expression 'γ max_Nsup_base(S_in)' is ill-formed); Eq. (6) describes 'dropping' via a sampling distribution whose direction (dropping low- vs high-prior references) is confusingly specified; citations include clearly erroneous entries (e.g., 'Constituency Parsing, 2009. Speech and language processing. Power point slides' cited for perplexity; 'GLM et al., 2024' as an author; a mangled Linq-Embed-Mistral citation), indicating careless preparation.
The abstract states 'The code is released at' with no URL; reproducibility of the full 15-LLM evaluation pipeline is therefore unverified.

Baseline settings are not uniformly tuned: e.g., 'Self-Consistency (Best on Validation)' uses per-dataset best-model selection, while other baselines use fixed aggregators; whether the gap (+4.31%) is attributable to RPS/EPE rather than aggregation budget (n=8 aggregations vs 8 samples) is not isolated.

The perplexity-based exploitation score (S_PPL = 1 − PPL, Appendix A.7) mixes unnormalized quantities with similarity scores in [0,1]; the authors argue the mismatch is benign empirically, but this is an ad hoc heuristic rather than a justified scoring function.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation: eight benchmarks spanning four task categories, fifteen open-source LLMs, comparisons against closed-source flagships (GPT-4.1, GPT-o3-mini, Claude) and six collaboration baselines (Symbolic-MoE, MoA, Self-MoA, Self-Consistency, Majority Voting, Simple Router).

Strong reported results: SMCS exceeds the per-dataset open-source upper bound (+2.86%) and leading closed-source models, with supporting cost and latency analysis (Table 2) showing the gains are not simply bought with disproportionate compute.

Thorough supporting analyses: component ablation (Table 10), accuracy-vs-cost curves over K, n, and N_sup_base (Tables 11-13), OOD question-bank experiments (Tables 3 and 7), retrieval composition analysis (Fig. 5), pairwise ranking score for prior-selection quality (Table 4), perplexity-scale analysis (Table 8), and multi-seed statistical analysis (Table 9).
Reproducibility support: code released, detailed dataset splits, full LLM bank specification (Table 5), inference configs, hyperparameters, and prompts (Appendix A.1-A.11).
Scalability claim is empirically grounded: performance consistently improves as the LLM pool grows from 5 to 15 models (Fig. 4), directly supporting the paper's central scalability argument.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the RPS module is essentially kNN routing over question embeddings with historical correctness scores, closely related to benchmark-based routing (Shnitzer et al., 2023); EPE is largely MoA-style multi-agmentation plus a perplexity/similarity selection score. The contribution is a reasonable engineering combination rather than a new technique, and the paper overstates novelty ('we first present a comprehensive analysis...').

Potential train-test proximity: the question bank is built from validation sets of the same benchmarks used for testing (e.g., MMLU-Pro validation stratified from the same distribution, MATH validation from the original dataset, AIME validation = historical problems), so retrieval may surface near-duplicate questions and inflate headline results. The OOD experiment (Table 3) partially mitigates this concern, but the marginal drops warrant more scrutiny and discussion.

Ablation gains are small while headline gains are large: individual components contribute roughly +0.5-1.5% each (Table 10), yet SMCS beats strong baselines by +4-6%; the paper does not clearly explain where the remaining improvement originates, and 'Self-Consistency (Best on Validation)' baseline selection is not fully specified.

Several methodological details are opaque or under-justified: whose model computes perplexity for the PPL score; how the balance coefficient λ=1.0 was chosen; how hyperparameters (K=7, n=8, γ=0.95) were tuned (presumably on validation, but unstated); Eq. (3) notation is inconsistent (I vs I_sup).

Presentation quality issues: notable typos and grammatical problems ('a embed', 'It explore diverse...', 'causes unfiltered low-quality responses as bottlenecks, which which'), and citation hygiene problems (e.g., 'Parsing, 2009' cited for perplexity; garbled author list for the Linq-Embed-Mistral reference).
Some results rest on small test sets (AIME 2024, n=30; GPQA-Diamond, n=198), making per-dataset claims fragile; statistical analysis covers only four of eight datasets.
